title: Power-sharing — Chapter Summary
intro: Belgium and Sri Lanka are small countries with sharp ethnic divisions. Belgium built a complex but stable model of power-sharing among its Dutch, French and German-speaking communities. Sri Lanka, by contrast, ruled by the SINHALA majority alone — and slid into a long civil war. The chapter draws from these two cases a single big idea: in a democracy, power must be SHARED. It explains why power-sharing is desirable and the four major forms it takes in modern democracies.

branches.label: Belgium
details: Equal ministers + state govts + community govt

sections.heading: Belgium and Sri Lanka
bullets: Belgium — a small European country with Dutch (59%), French (40%) and German (1%) speakers.
In Brussels, French-speakers are 80%, Dutch-speakers 20% — reverse of the country.
Tensions arose because the minority French-speakers were richer and more powerful.
Sri Lanka — Sinhala (74%) and Tamil (18%) communities; further split into Sri Lankan and Indian Tamils.
Most Sinhalese are Buddhist; most Tamils Hindu or Muslim; ~7% Christians.

sections.heading: Majoritarianism in Sri Lanka
bullets: Sri Lanka became independent in 1948.
1956 Act made SINHALA the only official language.
Preferential policies favoured Sinhala in jobs and universities.
Constitution made the state protect and foster Buddhism.
Tamil demands for autonomy were denied; by the 1980s they demanded a separate Tamil EELAM.
Civil war until 2009 — thousands killed, families displaced, severe setback to the country.

sections.heading: Accommodation in Belgium
bullets: Belgium amended its constitution 4 times between 1970 and 1993.
EQUAL Dutch / French ministers in the central government; some laws need majority of each language group.
Strong STATE GOVERNMENTS (Flemish, Walloon) — NOT subordinate to the centre.
Brussels has its own government with EQUAL representation of both communities.
A unique 'COMMUNITY GOVERNMENT' for each language community handles culture, education and language.
Brussels chosen as the headquarters of the European Union.

sections.heading: Why Power-sharing is Desirable
bullets: PRUDENTIAL reason — reduces conflict between social groups; ensures political stability.
MORAL reason — power-sharing is the VERY SPIRIT of democracy.
Tyranny of the majority is oppressive for the minority and ultimately ruins the majority too.
People have a right to be CONSULTED on how they are governed.

sections.heading: Forms of Power-sharing
bullets: HORIZONTAL — among legislature, executive and judiciary; system of CHECKS AND BALANCES.
VERTICAL — between central government and state / regional governments.
Among different SOCIAL GROUPS — e.g. Belgium's community government; reserved constituencies for SC/ST in India.
Among POLITICAL PARTIES, pressure groups and movements — coalition governments; interest-group influence.

key_takeaways: Belgium accommodated diversity through power-sharing; Sri Lanka used majoritarianism and faced civil war.
Belgium's constitution requires equal Dutch–French ministers, strong state governments, equal Brussels representation and a unique community government.
Sri Lanka's 1956 Sinhala-only law, preferential jobs/universities and pro-Buddhism constitution alienated the Tamil minority.
The Sri Lankan civil war ended in 2009 after huge social, cultural and economic damage.
Two reasons for power-sharing: PRUDENTIAL (better outcomes) and MORAL (spirit of democracy).
Tyranny of the majority hurts everyone in the long run.
Four forms of power-sharing: horizontal (organs), vertical (levels), social groups, political parties.

glossary.definition: Distributing political power among different organs of government, levels of government, social groups and political parties.
A belief that the majority community should rule the country in any way it wants, disregarding the wishes of any minority.
Relating to a common cultural, racial or linguistic identity within a population.
A violent conflict between organised groups within a country that becomes so intense it appears like a war.
A government formed by an alliance of two or more political parties, usually after no party wins a majority alone.
A system in which different organs of government can check the actions of one another, preventing concentration of power.
Power-sharing among organs of government at the same level — legislature, executive and judiciary.
Power-sharing across levels of government — central, state and local.
In Belgium, a government elected by people of one language community (Dutch / French / German) that handles cultural, educational and language matters.
Constituencies in legislatures reserved for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes or other specified groups.
A practical reason for power-sharing: it reduces conflict and ensures political stability.
A principled reason for power-sharing: it is the very spirit of democracy that people be consulted.
The separate state demanded by Sri Lankan Tamil organisations in the north and east of the island.
A political system with power constitutionally divided between a central government and regional governments.
An economic and political union of 27 European countries; its headquarters is in Brussels, Belgium.
